hypotheses.justification: hU appears only in the proof, through `leftArrow`, `leftArrow_unit` and `globalArrow_*`. The statement never mentions it, and it only concerns π₁ at p ∈ U ⊓ V. It can be dropped because U ⊓ V is path-connected (hI) and contains p. Let X' be the path component of p in X. Take a path γ from p. By the Lebesgue number lemma, γ splits into finitely many pieces, each lying in U or in V. Adjacent pieces of different type meet at a point of U ⊓ V, and merging same-type neighbours means every breakpoint lies in U ⊓ V. Each piece is a path in U (or V) with endpoints in U ⊓ V. Those endpoints lie in the path component U_p (resp. V_p) of p, because U ⊓ V is path-connected and contains p. Hence X' ⊆ U_p ∪ V_p. Also U ∩ X' = U_p, since any point of V_p ∩ U lies in U ⊓ V ⊆ U_p. Likewise V ∩ X' = V_p, and U_p ∩ V_p = U ⊓ V. So X' is covered by the open subsets U_p and V_p of X'. These are path-connected, and so is their intersection. The standard van Kampen theorem applies to X', with π₁(X',p) = π₁(X,p), π₁(U_p,p) = π₁(U,p) and π₁(V_p,p) = π₁(V,p). The same argument works if only hU is removed and hV is kept. A proof would reduce to the path component of p, or redo the open-cover argument with the arrows `leftArrow` etc. built only for the component of p. The ∃! statement stays true. hcover and hI are still needed, since without them the statement is false (for example, the circle covered by two arcs).

hV is symmetric to hU. It is used only in the proof, through `rightArrow`, `rightArrow_unit` and `globalArrow_*`, and does not occur in the statement. With hI (U ⊓ V path-connected, containing p) and hcover, every path in X from p decomposes into pieces in U or V with breakpoints in U ⊓ V. So the path component X' of p in X is contained in U_p ∪ V_p, with U ∩ X' = U_p, V ∩ X' = V_p and U_p ∩ V_p = U ⊓ V. Here U_p and V_p are the path components of p in U and V, and they are open in X'. Van Kampen for X' with this path-connected open cover gives the unique factorisation, and the π₁ groups at p of X', U_p, V_p equal those of X, U, V. So the ∃! statement holds without hV, whether or not hU is kept. Only the proof needs reworking, by reducing to the path component. Removing hU and hV together also works, by the same argument.
